heading: STEM apprenticeship programs

tree.heading: In general
tree.text: The Secretary of Commerce may carry out a grant program to identify the need for skilled science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (referred to in this section as “STEM”) workers and to expand STEM apprenticeship programs.

tree.heading: Eligible recipient defined
tree.text: In this section, the term “eligible recipient” means—

children.text: a city or other political subdivision of a State;

is a nonprofit organization, an institution of higher education, a public-private partnership, a science or research park, a Federal laboratory, or an economic development organization or similar entity; and
has an application that is supported by a State, a political subdivision of a State, or a native organization; or
a consortium of any of the entities described in paragraphs (1) through (5).

tree.heading: Needs assessment grants
tree.text: The Secretary of Commerce may provide a grant to an eligible recipient to conduct a needs assessment to identify—

children.text: the unmet need of a region’s employer base for skilled STEM workers;
the potential of STEM apprenticeships to address the unmet need described in paragraph (1); and
any barriers to addressing the unmet need described in paragraph (1).

tree.heading: Apprenticeship expansion grants
tree.text: The Secretary of Commerce may provide a grant to an eligible recipient that has conducted a needs assessment as described in subsection (c)(1) to develop infrastructure to expand STEM apprenticeship programs.

notes.heading: Developing STEM Apprenticeships
notes.text: Pub. L. 114–329, title III, § 312(a)–(d), Jan. 6, 2017, 130 Stat. 3013, 3014, provided that: “(a) Findings.—Congress makes the following findings:“(1) The lack of data on the return on investment for United States employers using registered apprenticeships makes it difficult—“(A) to communicate the value of these programs to businesses; and “(B) to expand registered apprenticeships. “(2) The lack of data on the value and impact of employer-provided worker training, which is likely substantial, hinders the ability of the Federal Government to formulate policy related to workforce training. “(3) The Secretary of Commerce has initiated—“(A) the first study on the return on investment for United States employers using registered apprenticeships through case studies of firms in various sectors, occupations, and geographic locations to provide the business community with data on employer benefits and costs; and “(B) discussions with officials at relevant Federal agencies about the need to collect comprehensive data on—“(i) employer-provided worker training; and “(ii) existing tools that could be used to collect such data. “(b) Development of Apprenticeship Information.—The Secretary of C
